metadata.title: Science teachers’ satisfaction: Evidence from the PISA 2015 teacher survey

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2015 teacher questionnaire data linked with PISA 2015 student and school questionnaires. Teachers are sampled within schools (science teachers and non-science teachers as two independently sampled populations), and because there is no teacher–student link, most analyses aggregate student data to the school level while keeping teacher-level outcomes. The paper states that all findings are weighted using a transformed version of the student weights, with construction described in Annex A; this implies complex survey weighting to support population-representative estimates across the 19 participating countries/economies. Malaysia is excluded from all-country averages and figures due to a low weighted response rate in sampled schools, so weighting and comparability are applied only to the remaining 18 participating countries/economies.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: This OECD report focuses on teacher satisfaction indices derived from teacher Likert items and related questionnaire indices (e.g., teacher collaboration, disciplinary climate perceptions). The dependent variables are not cognitive achievement scores generated via PISA plausible values, so PV handling is not applicable to the satisfaction outcomes. The report includes a section on missing data, but it does not provide a specific, mappable missing-data method in the extracted text, so the missing-data handling strategy cannot be classified from the provided material.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The analytic focus is science teachers in PISA 2015 teacher questionnaire participants across 19 countries/economies, with Malaysia excluded from all-country averages and figures due to a low weighted response rate among initially sampled Malaysian schools (51% vs. 85% standard). Teachers are sampled within each school: up to 10 science teachers are randomly sampled if a school has more than 10 science teachers; otherwise all science teachers are selected. In smaller schools, all science teachers are included. Non-responding teachers are those selected but not participating; the paper reports total responding science teachers and non-science teachers, and analyses are based on the teacher database with outcomes at the teacher level and (for most analyses) student and school variables aggregated to the school level.

data.outcome_summary: This OECD report analyzes how teacher, student, and school characteristics relate to science teachers’ satisfaction using PISA 2015. PISA 2015 is a triennial assessment of 15-year-olds, with science as the major domain and additional minor domains; the teacher questionnaire was administered for the first time in 19 participating countries/economies. The teacher satisfaction outcome is measured via eight Likert statements and summarized into two IRT-scaled indices: satisfaction with the teaching profession and satisfaction with the current job. Because there is no teacher–student link, most models aggregate student questionnaire variables to the school level while retaining teacher-level outcomes, and all results are weighted using transformed student weights. The report emphasizes that, in non-experimental cross-sectional data, associations cannot be interpreted causally due to non-random teacher–school selection and potential reverse causation.
data.null_fields_interpretation: This is an OECD descriptive/associational large-scale assessment report rather than an empirical machine-learning paper. The extracted text does not document any ML model training or predictive algorithm evaluation, and the outcomes are questionnaire-based satisfaction indices rather than PV-based achievement targets. Therefore, ML technique fields and structured predictive main findings are intentionally left empty, while the report’s methodological emphasis is on survey design, index construction, and correlational policy implications.
